title: Evolving Infra: An inference framework that adapt to dynamic agent workload
story_key: story|title:evolving infra an inference framework that adapt to dynamic agent workload
content_excerpt: This is an agent-native repository. Use your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, ...) to understand, deploy, benchmark and develop Evolving Infra. It reads AGENTS.md for the rules and the map of the code, and follows a skill for each task. Evolving Infra is an LLM serving system that adapts itself to the agent workload purely online , with no offline profiling . Serving coding, math and computer-use agents with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, it reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 4.1× and P95 time to first token by up to 14× compared with NVIDIA Dynamo , with up to 2.7× its throughput. Math (Putnam), coding (Claude Code) and computer-use (OSWorld) agents, three concurrency levels each. Lower is better. The router sends each request to a prefill node and a decode node. The planner moves nodes between the two groups (dashed arrow). KV stays in shared host memory while an agent branch still uses it. Architecture describes the request path. Evolving Infra is set up and run by your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, ...): each task below is a skill that the agent follows step by step, checking each step and reporting what it ran. Every component is in the runtime image, built for x86_64 (H200, B300) and aarch64 (GB300): docker.io/weili0234/evolving-infra:v0.1.0 . Ask your agent: "Reproduce the paper's Claude Code result on our Slurm cluster, following skills/run-benchmark/SKILL.md ." Give it the workload (Claude Code, Putnam or OSWorld), the Slurm account and partition, the image, the model directory and a directory every node sees. A run holds nine GPU nodes for about two hours. The workloads and the paper's results are in benchmarks/ . When a run does not start, fails a request or scores below the reference, ask it to follow skills/diagnose-run/SKILL.md . Join the InferenceRSI community to discuss the project, on Discord or in the WeChat group: MIT ( LICENSE ). The engine ( evolving_infra/engine/ ) and the router core ( evolving_infra/router/core/ ) are derived from SGLang at upstream commit 9a489f8d2f and, with Trie ( benchmarks/trie/ ), stay under the Apache License 2.0 in their own LICENSE files; NOTICE lists every included third-party work.

title: Your Coding Agent Can Read the Code. Give It the History with Relate by Neo4j
story_key: story|title:your coding agent can read the code give it the history with relate by neo4j
content_excerpt: AI and graph technologies give agents the understanding they need to generate trustworthy outputs, and humans the understanding they need to make better decisions. Discover how to model a knowledge graph, retrieve context with GraphRAG, connect agents with MCP, and build trustworthy AI that reasons over connected data. Load a repository’s git history into a graph with Relate’s git-to-graph extension, serve it read-only, and see what a coding agent finds with it that it cannot find in the source tree. In a popular open source codebase, security/api_key.py has been changed in 28 commits. In 18 of them oauth2.py changed too. http.py changed in 17, and open_id_connect_url.py in 16. None of those four modules imports another so nothing obvious in api_key.py points you at the other three files. The history is clear about why. Each time someone added a behavior to one security scheme, they added it to all of them: auto_error in #134, description in #1757, the 401 status code in #13786, WebSocket support in #10147. We asked three coding agents what else they would need to change before adding a constructor argument to APIKeyHeader . With only the source tree to read, none of them named those three modules. With the repository’s history loaded into a graph, all three did. This post shows how to build that graph with Relate’s git-to-graph extension , what to ask it, and what changed when Codex, OpenCode and Pi could query it. Relate is an open-source graph database built for AI agents to use directly. It is embedded: one binary, no server to deploy and no signup, and a whole database is a single .rl file on your machine that your agent queries in Cypher. “Agent-native” means the pieces an agent needs come with it. relate skill install gives a coding agent a skill that documents the CLI, its Cypher dialect and includes a catalog of ready-made queries. relate serve — mcp exposes any database as MCP tools, and --read-only makes it refuse every write. Relate extensions can be used to load outside data into the graph. This post uses two of them, git-to-graph for a repository’s history and fs-to-graph for its working tree . git-to-graph reads a checkout’s commit history. fs-to-graph reads its working tree. Both write into the same Relate store, so one graph holds what the code is and how it got there. title: Five agent chores: $258 on a top model, $11 on open models
story_key: story|title:five agent chores 258 on a top model 11 on open models
content_excerpt: Four of the five moved without one wrong answer. The fifth should stay where it is. We ran five routine AI jobs on a top closed model and on two open models. A month of that work cost $258.53 on Claude Sonnet 5.5. It cost $11.04 on the cheapest setup that got every answer right. Four of the five jobs moved without one wrong answer. The fifth did not, and it should stay where it is. An AI agent re-reads its whole instruction book every time it does anything. In this test that book was about 14,000 tokens, roughly 20 pages. Claude Sonnet 5.5 billed about 20,000 input tokens on each call. At $2 per million input tokens, each call costs about 4 cents before the model answers. A check that runs every 30 minutes is 1,440 calls a month. That is $57.57 a month, mostly to hear "nothing new". The open models charge far less for the same pages. gpt-oss-120b lists at $0.03 per million input tokens. DeepSeek V4 Pro lists at about $0.66. A call that cost 4 cents on Claude Sonnet 5.5 cost about a fifth of a cent on DeepSeek V4 Pro and about a twentieth of a cent on gpt-oss-120b. The baseline was Claude Sonnet 5.5, five runs per job. The open side was gpt-oss-120b and DeepSeek V4 Pro, ten runs per job each, on the two cheapest hosts our nightly grades allow. Temperature was zero. Code graded every answer against a stated answer. No model graded another model. The whole test billed $1.29. The rule for moving a job: the cheapest model that got every run right. The winning price for each job is in bold. The mix costs $11.04 a month. That saves $247.49 against Claude Sonnet 5.5 on everything. Note what the rule does. gpt-oss-120b was cheapest on the status check, but it missed one run in ten. So the status check goes to DeepSeek V4 Pro at $2.65. Cheapest is not the goal. Cheapest that passes is. The inbox digest failed on both open models. gpt-oss-120b returned no action emails at all on 3 of 10 runs. DeepSeek V4 Pro missed on 1 of 10. This job is different from the other four. The digest costs $6.06 a month on Claude Sonnet 5.5. Moving it would save under $6 and risk a missed email. Leave it. Settings broke more than models did. summary: LangSmith Tool Gateway, now in Public Beta, handles credentials, identity, and access for every agent tool call, with policies, approvals, and traces.
story_key: story|title:langsmith tool gateway secure governed tool use for agents
content_excerpt: Agents are moving beyond the chat window to take on more proactive and ambient work. Instead of waiting for a prompt, they run on a schedule or are triggered by events, and they’re handling longer tasks without someone checking every step. That makes them much more useful, but it also means teams need to control which tools each agent can call and whose identity it acts with, and keep a record of every action it takes. Today, we’re launching LangSmith Tool Gateway in Public Beta, on the LangSmith Agent Platform . Tool Gateway is a managed tool layer that handles credentials, identity, and access for every agent tool call, making it simple to govern the actions your agents take. Tool Gateway makes it easier and faster for engineering teams to grant agents access to new tools in a controlled manner and without hand-rolling auth each time. Security and compliance teams can use LangSmith to trace and audit tool calls as part of agent monitoring. When agents are in production, platform teams need visibility into what each agent did, controls over which tools and models it can use, and usage policies that limit spend and risk. With LangSmith, developers can build, run, and improve agents in a single platform. LLM Gateway governs the model calls agents make. With it, you can set spend limits and model fallbacks, add rate limits, redact personal data and secrets, and provides visibility within the agent trace with rich information on model calls such as latency, fallbacks, failures, guardrails triggered, etc. Tool Gateway lives in LangSmith alongside LLM Gateway, and provides governance across this lifecycle. Tool Gateway simplifies tool lists for agents, implementing policies on usage, managing identity for tool use, and as with LLM Gateway, provides visibility within the agent trace through rich information on tool calls such as servers, users, outcomes, latency, etc. Together, Tool Gateway and LLM Gateway provide comprehensive visibility and governance over agent actions and spend. Agents in production need to serve hundreds or thousands of users, each with their own set of permissions. This means managing and refreshing a large volume of tokens, and carefully managing and recording access for security and audit requirements. Managing identity and visibility at scale is orders of magnitude more difficult than local development. title: Genie One Accuracy: Why Curated Agents Need Governed Context
summary: Ask Finance and Underwriting whether the loss ratio improved from 2024 to 2025, and...
story_key: story|title:genie one accuracy why curated agents need governed context
content_excerpt: What 125 insurance questions taught us about routing, business definitions, and documents Ask Finance and Underwriting whether the loss ratio improved from 2024 to 2025, and you will get two contradictory answers that are both correct. In a fictional commercial auto insurer we built for this test, Finance reported an 8.2 percentage-point deterioration, and Underwriting reported a 1.5 percentage-point improvement. Neither was wrong. Finance tracks the calendar year net of reinsurance, so an adverse reserve development on an older claim shows up in today's numbers. Underwriting looks strictly at the policy year, gross of reinsurance and excluding catastrophes, because that's the baseline used to set rates. Reserving, meanwhile, relies on a third metric entirely: the accident-year ultimate loss ratio. The SQL can be perfectly correct and still produce an answer that doesn't make sense for the person asking. The challenge is knowing which business definition to apply when the same term has several valid definitions, while keeping shared facts, such as total policies written, consistent. This is the problem we wanted to explore with Genie One. Genie One, powered by Genie Ontology (now Generally Available), brings this business context into the analytics experience. Genie Ontology learns from the work teams already do, automatically capturing business logic, calculations, and relationships from existing dashboards, queries, notebooks, and semantic models as Ontology Snippets. This learned knowledge is complemented by modeled knowledge: explicitly defined, governed business concepts represented in Unity Catalog through certified Metric Views, Domains and Subdomains, and Pages. In this study, we refer to this modeled knowledge as the “governed layer”. Together, learned and modeled knowledge give Genie a richer understanding of how an organization works. Teams can build on the knowledge already captured from their existing assets, while using modeled knowledge to establish authoritative definitions for the business concepts where consistency and precision matter most. There is no need to model every concept upfront. This study explores a different aspect of Genie Ontology than the Turing benchmark described in our Genie Ontology GA announcement . title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
summary:
PostgreSQL 19 Released

Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse.

This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one:

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

In practice, that looks like this:

UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();

That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do:

WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time.

I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication:

In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it.

Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to MASTER_POS_WAIT().

Via Lobste.rs

title: How Abundant designed efficient rollout architecture with Modal Sandboxes
summary: Abundant builds RL environments that run on Modal Sandboxes, powering training for frontier labs.
story_key: model:modal|title:how abundant designed efficient rollout architecture with modal sandboxes
content_excerpt: Abundant builds reinforcement learning environments that frontier labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta use to train and evaluate their models. Labs improve agent capability by giving them difficult tasks that Abundant designs, letting the model attempt it, and grading the result as pass or fail. Each task is an RL rollout with a full environment. The model needs instructions, a defined goal, and a verifier to decide whether the task was completed. But it also needs infrastructure: compute to power the run, Dockerfiles, and isolation. Depending on the task, an agent may even need accelerators like GPUs. Abundant has created over 75,000 rollouts — ranging from GPU kernel optimization to long-horizon coding — each of which runs in a Modal Sandbox. Modal makes their rollout infrastructure easy to build and cost-efficient to run, enabling the Abundant team to focus on their core business. Today, almost all of Abundant’s rollout platform runs on Modal. Modal Functions power Abundant’s scheduler API to start tasks, clean up dead runs, and review rollouts. Modal Sandboxes power the rollout environments. Abundant initially chose to evaluate Sandbox providers because they wanted to avoid managing EC2 clusters directly, which would pull engineering time away from their core business of building RL environments. Modal enabled them to build their infrastructure directly in code, launch Sandboxes easily via API, and elastically scale their traffic as business grew. As of November 2026, Abundant runs over two million Sandboxes per month. Modal worked with the Abundant team to design and build their rollout architecture, focusing on designing a system that didn’t leave Abundant having to pay heavily for idle compute. Each rollout has a few steps: launch the task, attempt the task, verify the work, and report the work. Throughout the rollout, a “monitor” needs to verify that the Sandbox is still active. While Abundant had considered hosting the monitor outside of the Sandbox, they ultimately chose to include the rollout monitor inside the Sandbox and then used short-lived Modal Functions to start Sandboxes. The small rollout monitor inside the Sandbox makes periodic HTTP calls: a heartbeat every 30 seconds, live events, and the final result. If a Sandbox goes quiet, the control plane will attempt to connect three times before terminating it. title: Keeping Agents Fast: High-Interactivity Decode with FlyDSL MonoKernels in vLLM
summary: How FlyDSL MonoKernels keep agents responsive with high-interactivity decode in vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs, using model-specific fusion, data-ready handoffs, and specialized-decode integration.
story_key: model:vllm|title:keeping agents fast high interactivity decode with flydsl monokernels in vllm
content_excerpt: Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how MonoKernels written in FlyDSL reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. A MonoKernel combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, mono means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by TileRT , the implementations discussed here use a persistent launch : a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. Both paths in Figure 2 can be replayed under HIP graphs. The difference is between multiple independent kernels and an author-designed persistent schedule within a launch. Some whole-kernel boundaries become finer-grained handoffs between portions of the computation. content_excerpt: Coding is the largest category of enterprise AI application spend, reaching $34B in 2026 . Every company now wants to know what all that spend returns, but most engineering leaders still can’t give an exact answer to what it's buying. To try to understand coding agent ROI, teams used to look at high-level data like usage analytics and AI consumption, but these don’t provide insight into what tokens actually produce. Answering the ROI question is hard and requires visibility into spend across users and teams, along with a way to connect it to outcomes. We felt this friction firsthand when spend with our own coding agent, Robin, started climbing, and is one of the reasons we built a model router. Now we're excited to offer a practical solution for our customers too. LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce. This provides a clearer way to calculate the ROI behind coding agent budgets and understand how changes to models and policies impact it. The new LangSmith Agent Platform operates around the agent. Each agent has its own record and belongs to an "agent type" that determines what its dashboard shows, which data it connects to, and how it's evaluated. Coding agents are the first specialized agent type, and present data on pull requests, one of the signs that the agent's work is useful. LangSmith already traces coding agents across model providers, including Claude Code and Codex . With coding agents in LangSmith, the spend in each trace is automatically attributed to pull requests each agent contributed to. The attribution reflects the tasks a coding agent is used for. It covers both cases where a single thread can open several PRs, and where a PR can take several threads to finish, so data in LangSmith reflects what your agents actually accomplished and what it cost. Up until today, LangSmith enabled you to see the cost per trace for any of your coding agents, one trace at a time. This is useful for manual debugging, but doesn't provide visibility into trends across the entire team. The new coding agent overview page aggregates those costs and ties them to the pull requests your agents worked on. The dashboard shows KPIs at a glance, and clicking any metric opens its trend over time. For example, if your team switched models, you can compare before and after to see the impact of the change. title: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say
story_key: story|title:why your fine tuning job takes longer than the flops say
content_excerpt: Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs. A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models . The full version will be on arXiv soon. GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move. Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon. We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors. The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs. For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time: Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance. title: LoopCache: Accelerating Long-Context Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
summary: Looped Transformers achieve large effective depth with compact models by repeatedly applying a weight-shared block across R recurrent steps, each maintaining a loop-specific key-value (KV) cache. To accelerate sequential loop execution, recent wave-style self-speculative methods like WaveFront Decoding (WFD) and LoopSpec pipeline draft and target tokens across loops in a single step. However, they face two critical limitations. First, they draft only at fixed loops and ignore intermediate prediction changes, wasting computation on stale trajectories. Second, batching tokens from different loops loads up to Rx the KV cache per step, severely amplifying memory traffic in long-context scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose LoopCache, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for long-context Looped Transformers. Based on the correlation between prediction switches and output confidence, LoopCache introduces confidence-guided dynamic draft updating to refine drafts in flight across all intermediate loops. Furthermore, LoopCache employs a cyclic loop KV cache strategy that rotates through loop-specific KV caches, restricting per-step KV traffic to a single loop while batching tokens at the nearest matching cycle for lossless verification. By also selectively retaining independent KV caches for a few loop-sensitive shallow layers, LoopCache improves acceptance rates with negligible overhead. Experiments show that LoopCache achieves average 10.25x and 14.56x speedup over WFD and LoopSpec.

title: Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages
story_key: story|ver:0.5|variant:flash,speech|title:rumble 2 flash an open 0 5b speech model for 40 languages
content_excerpt: Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size. Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code . To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip. On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities. On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER . Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx . That's an hour of audio in about half a second. Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER , on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better. The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash . It's also available through our API . We're very curious what you'll b

content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. title: claude-code v2.1.325
summary:
What's changed

  • Fixed a security issue in how zstd-compressed responses are decoded
  • Added a spinner tip in VS Code and similar integrated terminals about re-running a notebook cell, shown once Claude has read or edited a Jupyter notebook
  • Added a line under the error shown when your organization's policy blocks a request, saying how to continue: run /rewind and change the message, or run /clear
  • Added a note for Claude when a sandboxed git checkout, git stash or autostash pull cannot update protected files such as those in .claude
  • Fixed /security-review and skills' inline git commands stopping with an error in worktrees of bare repositories, --separate-git-dir checkouts and Android repo checkouts
  • Fixed subagents with their own model being moved to the plan-mode model when the model setting is opusplan or haiku
  • Fixed subagents on a different model sizing file reads and MCP results with the main session's model
  • Fixed sessions on many third-party gateways and Foundry stopping with a context length error on every turn instead of compacting
  • Fixed recent turns sometimes going missing from a resumed session after Claude Code stopped without a clean exit
  • Fixed shell commands running in the launch directory after the working directory was deleted; the command now fails with a message and can be re-issued
  • Fixed an approved plan edit being lost when the plansDirectory folder can't take it: the plan is now saved in the default plans folder, and a warning says where and why
  • Fixed a saved sonnet[1m] model setting being rewritten on a new install to a model id the API rejects
  • Fixed focus view hiding the reply to your prompt when a scheduled task replied after it
  • Fixed the prompt sometimes missing from a background subagent's view when fullscreen is off
  • Fixed long options in lists and permission prompts being partly overwritten when they wrap, and first-run screens losing lines on narrow terminals
  • Fixed startup warnings about permission rules and the "N MCP servers need authentication" notice being recorded as seen when they were scrolled out of view
  • Fixed the welcome header showing control characters or splitting across lines when an agent's name or the working folder contains them or a line break
  • Fixed the red error shown when Claude tries a command only you can run: a dim line now says it runs only when you type it at the prompt
  • Fixed /stats showing an Active days total that was one day too high
  • Fixed /insights saying a report was ready when no session qualified for analysis, and writing two values into its HTML report without escaping them
  • Fixed /voice saying voice mode changed when managed settings, --settings, or the project's .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json kept it as it was; it now says what holds it
  • Fixed the IDE welcome dialog showing Cmd+Esc for Quick Launch on Windows and Linux
  • Fixed Slack app tips showing when your organization's policy denies cloud sessions
  • Fixed claude purge hanging silently when there is no terminal to read keys from, and its project picker and -i prompts ignoring the keyboard when stdin is piped
  • Fixed claude plugin eval --output-dir '' writing the report into the current folder; it now exits with an error
  • Fixed claude -p text output on a terminal passing control sequences other than text styling; pipes and files are unchanged
  • Fixed leftover .oauth_refresh.lock.owner.tmp.* files piling up in the config directory
  • Fixed /fast saying "Fast mode has been disabled by your organization" under the keyless Console sign-in, where Claude Code had not asked the server
  • Fixed /model saying that your organization restricts a model when Claude Code could not check that, for example with no network
  • Fixed "Sign in with your Console account" in /login replacing your existing login when you pressed Esc right after the browser step
  • Fixed the browser showing the sign-in success page in some cases where sign-in failed or was canceled
  • Fixed claude auth status and other short commands leaving a lock behind on a Console profile, which made the next session hang for about a minute
  • Fixed background sessions started on your claude.ai login using (and billing) an API key or token from the shell that started the background service
  • Fixed more cases of a session moving to another sign-in in the background; these moves are now refused, with a message saying what works
  • Fixed a second Enter in the exit dialog stopping background work after the move to the background was refused
  • Fixed token counting on Amazon Bedrock sending the conversation to Bedrock when the allowedProviders managed setting does not allow it
  • Fixed AWS credential_process helpers and Google Cloud default credentials failing when Claude Code is started without a HOME environment variable
  • Fixed a session sometimes going back to an earlier permission mode after a subagent's plan was approved
  • Fixed one invalid value in an Agent SDK applyFlagSettings() call silently discarding all settings from earlier calls; a call that would do this is now refused with an error
  • Fixed sessions showing as waiting for input when a finished pull request only needed your own review or merge
  • Fixed an unrecognized teammateMode settings value being ignored without a warning: claude -p, the startup warning and claude doctor now list it as a skipped entry (still not applied)
  • Fixed --worktree skipping a WorktreeCreate hook from a plugin in CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR on the first run in a new home directory
  • Fixed brief-mode sessions, such as Dispatch, sending a reply again after the turn had already replied
  • Fixed Claude saying a working Atlassian, Asana or Sentry connector had failed in cloud sessions when a plugin listed it at a different URL
  • Fixed Claude Desktop and SDK sessions listing a folder's own MCP servers (.mcp.json, local) as host-added or not at all, and not connecting WebSocket ones, after a folder move or pre-warmed start
  • Fixed /mcp still listing a plugin's MCP server after a plugin reload removed it while it was connecting
  • Fixed an MCP server staying "needs authentication", and its mcp_tool hooks being skipped, after a token refresh that was refused only for a moment
  • Fixed MCP elicitation requests being cancelled without asking in headless mode after a server's connection was replaced during a tool call
  • Fixed MCP tool calls from an SDK host answering "Not connected" after a tool call had reconnected the MCP server
  • Fixed an MCP task getting stuck after its question was closed with Esc or asked again: the footer now says it needs your input, and Enter in /tasks shows the question again
  • Fixed background MCP tasks that stopped updating after another call to the same server lost the connection, when a later call reconnects
  • Fixed a background MCP task's question opening over a message you were still typing; it now waits until you send or clear the draft, and the spinner and turn timer keep running
  • Fixed worktree.sparsePaths and sparse plugin and marketplace clones leaving out the repository's root files on older git versions, such as 2.34
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions with several repositories being unable to use a repository added mid-session
  • Fixed Claude asking for permission before reading your own artifact or its data
  • Fixed deny and ask permission rules and hooks for the Artifact tool not applying in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts ignoring a worktree entered with EnterWorktree, writing ~ paths into the project, and leaving /mcp showing an MCP server as connected after its sign-in expired
  • Fixed words typed with a Yes at a permission dialog or plan approval not reaching Claude in Code Mode
  • Fixed Claude starting work by itself when you resumed a session that ended during a Code Mode script; it now waits for your next prompt
  • Fixed a missing OpenTelemetry user_prompt event for a message sent while tool calls run. The event has delivery.mode: "mid_turn" and the running turn's prompt.id
  • Fixed the OpenTelemetry user_prompt event leaving out earlier messages' text when queued messages merged into one turn in VS Code, or when one message had an image
  • Fixed a slash command's allowed-tools grants applying to background agents woken during or after its turn
  • Fixed /feedback and /bug to upload other sessions only when they were recorded by the signed-in account or organization
  • Fixed relative deny and ask permission rules (e.g. Read(./.env)) no longer covering the project after a cd; they now also apply in added directories
  • Fixed deny and ask permission rules starting with mcp__plugin_*_ missing a plugin's MCP server or tool spelled in another letter case
  • Fixed deny rules not being applied to a permission approval that arrives after Claude Code restarts, in self-hosted runner and claude remote-control sessions
  • Fixed a case where a committed .claude/settings.local.json could be treated as the user's own when Claude Code was started in certain subfolders of a repository
  • Fixed some deny and ask rules not applying to certain Bash commands
  • Fixed a gap in Bash permission checks where some compound commands could run without asking; these now ask for permission
  • Fixed a case where a Bash allow rule could run a different program than the one it names
  • Fixed a connector tool's approval prompt in cloud sessions being answered automatically while plugins were still loading
  • Fixed some subagents changing an artifact that people outside your organization can see, or uploading files to it, without asking first when an allow rule is set or uploads were approved earlier
  • Fixed some artifact publishes skipping the confirmation for pages that people outside your organization can see when "don't ask again" had been chosen for Artifact
  • Fixed auto mode judging only the first change to an artifact that people outside your organization can see; its yes now covers that change alone
  • Fixed a managed strictPluginOnlyCustomization lock on agents and skills not taking effect in sessions that were already running
  • Fixed sandboxed commands being able to write to the native updater's download folder in some cases
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a worktree's settings and hooks
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a linked worktree's shared git folder
  • Fixed /teleport's stash choice in some unusual git states: it now stops and says what to do
  • Windows: Fixed a start-up stall that could last about a second when a PATH entry sits under a folder your account cannot open
  • Fixed /resume on Windows refusing or hiding sessions whose folder was recorded with a different drive-letter case or slashes
  • Fixed an in-session /resume on Windows dropping a project's saved trust when the session was recorded with a different drive-letter case
  • Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when the working directory was below an allowRead folder inside a denyRead, such as under a symlinked home directory
  • Fixed Claude Desktop's third-party deployments staying on "Stopping" until a token renewal finished (once it includes this version)
  • Improved subagents cut off at the output token limit: they are now asked for the whole answer again, more briefly, instead of returning only its end
  • Improved startup with a keyless Console sign-in or other Anthropic profile login: a token that is still valid is read without waiting for the credentials lock
  • Improved the account email check: it now also refuses your email as a client's identity in scripts a command runs, file writes, web fetches and MCP calls
  • Improved the HTTPS authentication failed message for private plugin marketplaces: it now says git's terminal prompts and askpass programs are disabled, and it also appears with newer git versions
  • Improved the add-marketplace confirmations, plugin recommendation prompts and plugin install warning to say that plugins can run code on your computer, with access to your files and shell
  • Improved the claude --desktop sign-in error to name the API key, provider or setting that stops a Claude account sign-in from working
  • Improved the /voice "No audio detected" message on macOS and Windows: it now says where to pick your microphone
  • Improved MCP tasks: Claude is now told when a task is waiting for your answer, and can point you to /tasks
  • Improved claude remote-control: it now exits with status 4 when it stops by itself (single-session runs still exit 0) and 69 when it can't register, so a service manager can start it again
  • Improved the messages shown when a background session can't use its session's API key or token: they no longer suggest adding the key to settings
  • Improved the bundled dataviz skill's part-to-whole advice for static images and for parts with a natural order, such as age bands
  • Changed sandboxed Bash commands to follow the normal permission flow by default; set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true to keep running them without prompts
  • Changed managed settings that turn the sandbox on: to keep commands running without prompts, set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true in your highest-ranking managed source
  • Changed read-only git commands to ask first in a repository that isn't the project's or one you trusted; name it with --add-dir, not the additionalDirectories setting, to run them without prompts
  • Changed scheduled tasks and /loop to ask before running a skill that declares allowed-tools or hooks; add Skill(name) to permissions.allow to run it unattended
  • Changed "Always allow" in Desktop, IDE and SDK hosts: a rule alone is offered only when saving it would allow that command again, so a scheduled task that relied on one can now wait for you
  • Changed the sandbox to refuse sandboxed writes to .claude settings, skills, agents, commands and hooks in added directories, as it does in the launch folder
  • Changed worktree isolation: an isolated worktree session or agent is now refused git bisect run, git maintenance register|start and scalar's set-up commands, and is told what still works
  • Changed plugin MCP bundles (.mcpb, .dxt) to unpack under the plugins directory, not .mcpb-cache in the plugin's folder, so read-only plugin folders load; one fetched by URL downloads again once
  • Changed plugins of a remote marketplace that managed settings declare, enable and list in prependPlugins or appendPlugins to count as the organization's; pluginDigests is deprecated and ignored
  • Changed plugin loading to skip, and claude plugin validate to report, some unsafe paths and links in a plugin's folder
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders in --plugin-dir plugins no longer load from a session started above them; start Claude Code in the plugin folder instead
  • Changed EnterWorktree to refuse a WorktreeCreate hook path that goes through a symlink inside the project; have the hook print the real path
  • Changed tmux and iTerm2 teammates, and new sessions from the agents view opened with ←, to start in the session's folder instead of where the shell last ran cd
  • Changed prompt suggestions in the terminal to refresh less often after 8 turns in a row started by background or scheduled tasks, saving usage until you press a key or return to the terminal
  • Changed Esc on a background MCP task's question to "answer later": nothing is sent to the server, and the question stays in /tasks
  • Changed CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS to also set the context window of unrecognized model IDs that start with claude-, such as a gateway's claude-sonnet-latest
  • Changed /login to ask for permission to change your privacy settings
  • Changed /cost, $.session.usage(), --max-budget-usd and the cost and token metrics to count a mod's $.model.complete and $.model.classify calls
  • Changed the programs that Claude Code's sandbox starts for its own use, such as its network bridge, to run without Claude Code's sign-in tokens and API keys in their environment
  • Changed ripgrep, local git commands and the sandbox runtime's own helper programs to run without the mTLS client key's passphrase in their environment
  • Remote Control: Changed /resume and /teleport to disconnect first when the connected session has a share link, or when that can't be checked; run /remote-control to connect again
  • Changed Claude Code on the web, cloud scheduled tasks and Cowork cloud sessions to start despite sandbox.failIfUnavailable: the hosted container has no command sandbox
  • Changed requests for settings, permission rules, hooks or status over a cloud or self-hosted session's connection to return less or be refused; what applies in the session is unchanged
  • Changed claude -p with no cached account data to wait for that data before its first request, so a first run in a clean environment can start a few seconds later
  • Changed Claude's instructions to keep files you'll want out of its temporary scratchpad folder, which can be cleared
  • Changed marketplace ref to accept the full ID of any commit on a branch or tag; clients before this version can't clone such a pin, so a marketplace pinned this way stops loading there
  • Changed plugin marketplace and plugin downloads to use a CONNECT tunnel when ALL_PROXY is the only proxy set; a proxy that refuses CONNECT now fails them
  • Changed -p and SDK runs in a worktree or submodule mounted into a container to apply .claude/settings.local.json allow rules only once the folder is trusted
  • Changed self-hosted runners to refuse a session whose session folder or repository path is a symbolic link, other than a checkout hook's checkout
  • Removed "ask your admin to raise it" from spend limit and shared budget errors in cloud sessions and under Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Added prompt suggestions wherever the terminal shows them: Tab accepts the suggested next prompt; promptSuggestionEnabled: false in Claude Code's settings.json turns them off
  • [VSCode] Added a Console sign-in that creates no API key
  • [VSCode] Added a field to paste the redirect URL when signing in to an MCP server from the panel in SSH, WSL and container windows
  • [VSCode] Fixed the model picker's check mark staying on the old model after Claude Code restarted on another model or the model was switched over Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Fixed the effort selector offering levels above the effort cap set by your organization or the maxEffortLevel setting
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen offering sign-ins that the managed allowedProviders setting refuses
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt for MCP tools not saying why Claude Code asks when a safety check raises the question
  • [VSCode] Fixed the message for organization settings that couldn't load saying to run a command again; it now says to try again, matching the tab's Retry link
  • [VSCode] Improved the note shown for an untrusted folder: it now says why the extension is off and how to turn it on

  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in card to say what to do when the browser shows a connection error for localhost
  • [VSCode] Changed the install link's marketplace confirmation button to "Trust marketplace and continue"
